title: Restrictions on Foreign Fund Flow to Christian Organizations in India Complicate India-US Ties
gist: India's FCRA Amendment Bill 2026, introduced in the Lok Sabha in March 2026, would let a new Ministry of Home Affairs-appointed 'designated authority' seize and dispose of an NGO's assets if its foreign-funding registration lapses; the bill drew enough criticism that parliament referred it to a 31-member joint committee on August 12, delaying a report until the winter session.

themes.theme: Tightening control over foreign funding of NGOs

insights.claim: The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment (FCRA) Bill, 2026 was introduced in the Lok Sabha, the lower house of India's Parliament, on March 25, 2026, to amend the FCRA Act 2010 which regulates the receipt and use of foreign contributions by individuals and organizations in India.
insights.speaker: Rushali Saha
insights.so_what: Marks a new round of legislative tightening on foreign funding into India, relevant to any NGO, faith-based organization, or foreign donor operating there.
insights.quote: On March 25, the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment (FCRA) Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha, the lower house of the Indian Parliament.

insights.claim: A key provision of the bill creates a 'designated authority' under India's Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) with power to provisionally take over, manage, and dispose of an organization's assets if its FCRA registration is canceled, surrendered, or undergoes 'deemed cessation' due to non-renewal.
insights.speaker: Rushali Saha
insights.so_what: Gives the Indian government direct asset-seizure power over NGOs whose foreign-funding registration lapses, a material compliance and expropriation risk for foreign-funded civil-society and religious organizations in India.
insights.quote: A key provision of the recent amendment bill relates to the creation of a “designated authority” under the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), which has been empowered to provisionally take over, manage, and dispose of the assets of an organization if its FCRA registration is canceled, surrendered, or undergoes “deemed cessation” due to non-renewal.
insights.locator: A key provision of the recent amendment

insights.claim: This asset-seizure provision has generated considerable criticism.
insights.speaker: Rushali Saha
insights.so_what: Domestic pushback signals possible amendments or delays before the bill's final form, a factor for organizations planning around the new rules.
insights.quote: This change has generated considerable criticism.

insights.claim: On August 12, 2026, India's parliament adopted a motion to refer the FCRA Amendment Bill to a 31-member joint parliamentary committee, which is to scrutinize the bill and submit its report in the first week of parliament's winter session.
insights.speaker: Rushali Saha
insights.so_what: The referral to committee pushes final passage into the winter session at the earliest, giving affected organizations a defined window to monitor and respond before the law takes effect.
insights.quote: On August 12, parliament adopted a motion referring the bill to a 31-member joint parliamentary committee, which will scrutinize the bill and submit its report in the first week of the parliament’s winter session.

insights.claim: The FCRA Act 2010 has already been amended three times, most recently in 2020, and the 2026 bill would mark a fourth round of changes.
insights.speaker: Rushali Saha
insights.so_what: A repeated pattern of amendments shows a sustained multi-year trend of India tightening rather than loosening control over foreign funding, useful context for forecasting future regulatory direction.
